unit.subject: English
unit.unitOverview: Unit 4 is about community and communication — the many ways people share news, ideas and help with one another. You will read about a library service that travels by cart, a young reporter called Maya, and a town meeting that opens a new community centre. You will learn words such as service, deliver, knowledge, information, discover and priority, and use them to talk and write about your own community. By the end you will share a message clearly, just as Amal does in this unit's story, “The Circular Plan”.
unit.learningPath:
Start with Vocabulary: learn four or five words each day, then do the practice sentences.
Work through the six grammar lessons, from countable nouns to imperatives and descriptive starters.
Read the three passages and the story “The Circular Plan”, then answer the comprehension questions.
Practise the six speaking tasks, draft the six writing tasks, and complete the six activities.
Finish with the quiz, the self-assessment and the unit portfolio assignment.

readings.title: The Library That Came to Us
readings.setting: A coastal town and familiar school contexts
readings.passageScript:
In a small town beside the warm sea, there is a library with a bright blue door. It is a plain white building, but inside it is full of treasure: shelves of fiction stories and shelves of true books packed with knowledge. Every morning, children from the town gather on the library steps before school, trading thoughts about the last chapter they read.

The librarian wanted every child to read, even the children who lived far from the town, in villages with no library of their own. So she began a new service. Every Thursday, she loads books into a cart and travels along the dusty road to the villages to deliver them. She checks the quality of every book before it goes into the cart, and she counts the quantity carefully so that nothing is lost on the journey.

“A library is not the building,” she says, resting a hand on the cart’s wooden wheel. “It is the books, and the people who read them. My priority is to bring information and good stories to everyone, wherever they live.”

The children wait beside the road and count the minutes until they hear the wheels creaking closer. When they discover a new book they love, their faces shine like the sea at sunrise. One boy always asks the same question: “Will you come again next Thursday?” The librarian always gives the same answer. “As long as there are readers waiting, I will always come back.”
readings.reviewStatus: Needs re-review (content updated for self-sufficiency pass)

readings.title: Maya the Young Reporter
readings.setting: A coastal town and familiar school contexts
readings.passageScript:
Maya is nine years old, and she wants to be a scientist one day. Right now, her biggest challenge is the class newspaper she writes every week for Teacher Yasmin’s class. Every Monday she opens her notebook, taps her pencil, and thinks of a good headline before she starts.

She must find real information about her town and share it clearly with her readers, so nobody is left confused. Last week, Maya learned that the population of her neighbourhood was growing, because many new families had arrived from the city to open new shops near the market.

“That is important news,” said Teacher Yasmin, reading over Maya’s shoulder. “Write it clearly, and do not judge the new families — welcome them, and ask them what they hope to discover here.”

Maya wrote her report neatly, choosing each word with care. She was careful to erase every mistake before she stuck the pages down onto the notice board, because a good reporter checks her own work twice.

Her friend Sami tried to tease her at first. “A newspaper written by a nine-year-old?” he laughed, leaning over her desk. But when he actually sat down and read it, word by word, he stopped teasing completely. “This is high-quality work,” he said, surprised. “Can I help you next week? I have an idea for a story too.”
readings.reviewStatus: Needs re-review (content updated for self-sufficiency pass)

readings.title: The Town Meeting
readings.setting: A coastal town and familiar school contexts
readings.passageScript:
“Good evening, everyone, and thank you for coming to the town hall tonight,” said the mayor, smiling at the rows of neighbours. “I want to share some information about our new community centre, which opens next month near the market square.

First, there is a reading room, and there are many books already stacked on the new shelves. Then, there is a small clinic, where a nurse will give health advice every morning. Finally, there is an open hall for meetings, lessons and community events. This whole centre is a service for all of us.”

A woman near the front raised her hand. “Will the reading room be open for children after school?” she asked.

“Yes,” the mayor replied. “Every child in the population of our town is welcome, and there is no priority list — everyone may come.”

An older man called out, “How will we know when it opens?”

“Please spread the news, tell your neighbours, and bring your ideas to the next meeting,” said the mayor. “Communication is how a community grows strong, and this centre belongs to every one of you.”

readings.title: The Circular Plan
readings.setting: A coastal town and familiar school contexts
readings.passageScript:
Amal lived in a small town beside the sea. Her school was plain on the outside, but it was full of energy inside. Every week, Teacher Yasmin gave the class a new challenge — something to learn or build together as a team.
One morning, Teacher Yasmin wrote on the board: “Project: Create a way to share information with the community.”
Amal raised her hand. “Do you mean a newspaper?”
“Something like that,” Teacher Yasmin said. “But you must use what you already know. Use your knowledge, and make something useful.”
The students talked during break. “We could build one enormous sign!” said Leo.
“No,” said Nora. “People will just walk past it. Let us make a box with papers inside.”
“That is still too plain,” Amal added. “It has to be circular. That is my rule!”
“Why circular?” Leo teased. “Is your brain a wheel?” Amal laughed, but she did not answer. She already had an idea.
After school, Amal went to the town library. She looked at the location of every fiction shelf, every news board, and every reading chair.
“We want to deliver news and stories to the whole town,” she told the librarian.
“That is a big job,” the librarian said kindly. “But good service always starts small.”
Amal walked home past the school gate and stopped. “Everybody passes this spot,” she whispered. “This is the right location.”
The next day, Amal and her friends arrived early. They brought cardboard, tape, scissors, and markers.
“What are you building?” asked a younger boy.
“A circular news station!” Amal answered. “People will stop here and spin the circle. Each part gives different information — the weather, stories, or health tips.”
Leo frowned. “That sounds hard.”
“It is a challenge,” Amal agreed. “But we can do it together.”
Teacher Yasmin came by and nodded. “Very creative,” she said. “Now check your spelling before you stick anything down. And do not forget to erase the pencil lines.”
The group worked neatly. Amal drew the circle. Leo wrote the headlines. Nora added a funny comic about a scientist and a dancing goat, and everyone laughed.
“We need facts too,” Amal said, “not just fiction.”
“There is a doctor in town,” said Leo. “Let us write about health.”
“There are new shops opening as well,” added Nora.
“Write clearly. That is our top priority,” Amal reminded them.
By Friday, the project was ready. They placed it near the school gate, where every parent and child walks past. It stood tall and colourful.
The next morning, a group of parents and children gathered around it. “What is this?” asked a man.
“It is called ‘The Circular Plan’,” Amal explained. “Turn it, and read what is on each side.”
A woman read aloud, “Tips for clean water.” A boy spun it and found the comic. “A goat that becomes a scientist?” he laughed.
“It is only fiction!” Leo shouted, grinning. People laughed and clapped. “This is good service,” someone said. “Our children are teaching us.”
One parent pointed. “But there is no news about the market. That is what people care about.”
“Then please help us write it!” Amal replied. “We want real thought from the people too.”
Another woman smiled. “That is a good priority — sharing everyone’s voice.”
Teacher Yasmin stood beside the project. “This,” she said, “is how we build a community. We learn, we teach, and we grow. Today, our students became leaders.”
As the crowd left, a boy began to tease Leo about his handwriting. “Your words look like little bugs!” he laughed. Leo grinned. “I wrote them in a hurry. I will fix them later.”
“Good idea,” said Amal. “We must always check for quality.”
That afternoon, Amal looked at the circle again. “It may look plain,” she said to Nora, “but the work inside it matters.”
Nora nodded. “It is not about how big the quantity is,” she said. “It is about what people learn.”
And from that day on, people in Amal’s town stopped by the spinning circle, learned something new, and sometimes even added their own page.

comprehension.question: What new service did the librarian begin, and how often does she carry it out?
comprehension.correctAnswer: She began taking books to the villages by cart, and she does it every Thursday.
comprehension.explanation: The passage names the new service and then gives the day, so both facts sit side by side.

comprehension.question: What is Maya's weekly challenge, and what job does she hope to do one day?
comprehension.correctAnswer: Her weekly challenge is the class newspaper, and she hopes to be a scientist one day.
comprehension.explanation: The opening lines give her ambition first and then name the challenge she meets each week.

comprehension.question: Name the three rooms the speaker describes inside the new community centre.
comprehension.correctAnswer: There is a reading room, there is a small clinic, and there is an open hall.
comprehension.explanation: The speaker lists the rooms with First, Then and Finally, so each connective marks one room.

comprehension.question: What project did Teacher Yasmin write on the board one morning?
comprehension.correctAnswer: She asked the class to create a way to share information with the community.
comprehension.explanation: The project is quoted word for word on the board, just after the class hears about the weekly challenge.

comprehension.question: The librarian says her priority is to bring two things to everyone. What are they?
comprehension.correctAnswer: Her priority is to bring information and good stories to everyone in the villages.
comprehension.explanation: She states her priority inside the quotation marks, straight after she explains what a library really is.

comprehension.question: What had happened to the population of Maya's neighbourhood, and what caused it?
comprehension.correctAnswer: The population was growing, because many new families had arrived in the neighbourhood.
comprehension.explanation: The sentence gives the change first and the cause second, joined by the connective because.

comprehension.question: Which three sequence connectives does the speaker use to put the three rooms in order?
comprehension.correctAnswer: The speaker uses First, Then and Finally to put the three rooms in order.
comprehension.explanation: Each connective opens a new sentence and is followed by a comma, which marks the next step of the tour.

comprehension.question: Where did Amal's group finally place The Circular Plan, and why did they choose that location?
comprehension.correctAnswer: They placed it near the school gate, because every parent and child walks past that spot.
comprehension.explanation: Amal studies the library first, then chooses the gate, and she gives her reason in a whisper.

comprehension.question: Why does the librarian say that a library is not the building?
comprehension.correctAnswer: She means the books and the readers matter far more than the plain white walls.
comprehension.explanation: Her very next sentence explains the idea, naming the books and the people who read them.

comprehension.question: How did Sami's opinion of the newspaper change, and what made him change it?
comprehension.correctAnswer: He stopped teasing and called it high-quality work once he had actually read it.
comprehension.explanation: The teasing comes first and the praise comes afterwards, with reading the report as the turning point.

comprehension.question: The speaker says there is a reading room but there are many books. Why does the verb change?
comprehension.correctAnswer: One reading room is singular, so it takes is, while many books is plural and takes are.
comprehension.explanation: There is introduces a single thing, and there are introduces two or more, so the verb has to change.

comprehension.question: What did Nora mean when she said it is not about how big the quantity is?
comprehension.correctAnswer: She meant that what people learn matters more than the number of pages on the circle.
comprehension.explanation: Nora sets quantity against learning in her closing line, which gives the whole story its message.

grammar.title: Countable and Uncountable Nouns
grammar.explanation: Some nouns can be counted one by one — one book, two books, three books — and we call these countable nouns. Other nouns cannot be split into separate items, such as water, rice or information, and we call these uncountable nouns. Knowing the difference tells you whether to reach for many or for much, so your sentences stay accurate.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
Countable nouns take a number, or many and few: “I have three apples.” “There are many books.”
Uncountable nouns take no number. Use much, little or some: “I need some water.” “We have much information.”
Use a or an only in front of a singular countable noun: “a book” is correct, but “a information” is not.
grammar.commonMistake: Learners often write, “Can you give me some informations?” Information is uncountable, so it never takes an “s”. The friendly fix is, “Can you give me some information?”
grammar.memoryTip: If you can put a number in front and add “s” (one apple, two apples), the noun is countable. If you would pour it or scoop it, like water, rice or sugar, it is almost always uncountable.
grammar.practice: Choose the correct word. | I have ______ (many / much) friends at school. | Could you give me ______ (some / many) information about the project? | There are ______ (few / little) biscuits left in the jar. | I would like ______ (a / an) orange, please. | We need ______ (much / many) chairs for the party. Self-check: 1) many, 2) some, 3) few, 4) an, 5) many.

grammar.title: There is / There are
grammar.explanation: We use there is and there are to say that something exists in a place. The pattern lets you describe your town and share information about everything around you, which is exactly what the town-meeting speaker does.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
There is introduces one single thing, or an uncountable noun: “There is a library.” “There is water in the glass.”
There are introduces two or more things: “There are three scientists in the laboratory.”
In a question the two words swap places: “Is there a clinic nearby?” “Are there many books?”
grammar.commonMistake: Learners often write, “There is two cats on the wall.” Cats is plural, so the sentence needs there are: “There are two cats on the wall.”
grammar.memoryTip: Picture one star shining alone for is, and a whole sky of stars twinkling together for are.
grammar.practice: Choose the correct phrase. | ______ a bird in the tree. (is / are) | ______ three cars in the car park. (is / are) | ______ an elephant at the zoo. (is / are) | ______ many students in the classroom. (is / are) | ______ some information on the noticeboard. (is / are). Self-check: 1) There is, 2) There are, 3) There is, 4) There are, 5) There is.

grammar.title: Present Simple (Facts)
grammar.explanation: We use the present simple for facts, habits and things that are always true, such as “Postal workers deliver letters daily.” It is the tense you need when you write a short report of true information about your own town.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
With I, you, we and they, use the base verb: “They deliver letters.” “I read books.”
With he, she and it, add -s or -es: “She plays.” “He watches.”
Time words sit comfortably beside facts: daily, often, every day, sometimes.
grammar.commonMistake: Learners often write, “She play football every day.” The subject is she, so the verb needs its “s”: “She plays football every day.”
grammar.memoryTip: He, she and it are the three little words that always ask the verb for its “s”. Everybody else keeps the plain base verb.
grammar.practice: Write the correct present simple form of the verb in brackets. | Dogs ______ (bark) when they see strangers. | She ______ (study) every day after school. | Fish ______ (swim) in water. | My brother ______ (play) football at the weekend. | The Earth ______ (revolve) around the Sun. Self-check: 1) bark, 2) studies, 3) swim, 4) plays, 5) revolves.

grammar.title: Passive Voice
grammar.explanation: In the active voice the subject does the action: “The cat chased the mouse.” In the passive voice the subject receives the action: “The mouse was chased by the cat.” Choose the passive when the action, or the person it happened to, matters more than the doer.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
Move the object to the front: “The teacher reads the book” becomes “The book …”
Add the correct form of to be — is, are, was or were: “The book is …”
Add the past participle of the verb: “The book is read …”
Add the doer with by only when your reader needs it: “The book is read by the teacher.”
grammar.commonMistake: Learners often write, “The meal is cook by the chef.” The passive needs the past participle: “The meal is cooked by the chef.”
grammar.memoryTip: Ask yourself, “What happens to the subject?” If the subject receives the action instead of doing it, you are looking at the passive voice.
grammar.practice: Change each active sentence into the passive voice. | The artist paints the picture. | The team won the game. | The students finished their homework. | The librarian delivers the books every Thursday. Self-check: 1) The picture is painted by the artist. 2) The game was won by the team. 3) Their homework was finished by the students. 4) The books are delivered by the librarian every Thursday.

grammar.title: Connectives of Sequence
grammar.explanation: Connectives of sequence show the order of steps or events — First, Next, Then, After that, Finally. They are what make a set of instructions, or a talk about a new community centre, easy for a listener to follow.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
Begin each step with a connective: First, … Then, … After that, … Finally, …
Put a comma straight after the connective when it opens the sentence.
Keep the steps in their true order so the reader never has to guess what comes next.
grammar.commonMistake: Learners often write, “First discover the problem.” The connective still needs its comma: “First, discover the problem.”
grammar.memoryTip: Treat the connectives as a treasure map: each one walks the reader to the next step, so never leave a step out.
grammar.practice: Fill each blank with a sequence connective (First, Next, After that, Finally). | ______, wash your hands. | ______, dry your hands with a towel. | ______, lay the plates on the table. | ______, enjoy your snack! Self-check: 1) First, 2) Next, 3) After that, 4) Finally.

grammar.title: Imperatives and Descriptive Starters
grammar.explanation: An imperative is a command that tells somebody what to do, such as “Sit down” or “Erase your mistakes”. A descriptive starter opens the sentence with a describing word beside its noun, so “The service is good” becomes “This high-quality service is very helpful.” Imperatives make instructions direct; descriptive starters make descriptions vivid.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
Imperative: use the base verb with no “to” — Clean. Erase. Listen.
Imperative: add detail, or please, when you want to sound warm — “Please erase your mistakes neatly.”
Imperative: open with Do not to say what to avoid — “Do not run in the hall.”
Descriptive starter: choose your noun, choose your describing word, and put the pair at the front — “This high-quality service …”
Descriptive starter: finish the thought so the sentence is complete — “This high-quality service is very helpful.”
grammar.commonMistake: Two slips are common here. Learners write, “To clean your room,” when an imperative needs the bare base verb: “Clean your room.” They also write, “This high-quality services are useful,” when a singular noun needs a singular verb: “This high-quality service is useful.”
grammar.memoryTip: An imperative begins with the action word itself, so it sounds like a friendly “do” instruction. A descriptive starter dresses the noun up, so picture the describing word as the smart coat your noun wears at the front.
grammar.practice: Part A — complete each command with the base form of the verb in brackets. | ______ (eat) your vegetables! | ______ (close) the window, please. | ______ (not talk) during the film. | ______ (help) your friend with the project. | ______ (bring) your book to class tomorrow. | Part B — add a describing word at the start of each sentence. | ______ dog is playful. | ______ book is interesting. | ______ game is exciting. Self-check for Part A: 1) Eat, 2) Close, 3) Do not talk, 4) Help, 5) Bring. Part B is open-ended, so there is no single fixed word — here are model examples: ‘A spotted dog is playful.’ ‘An old book is interesting.’ ‘A new game is exciting.’

speaking.title: Speaking 1: Describe a Service in Your Community
speaking.instructionsAndModelLines:
Think of a service in your community: a shop, a post office, a clinic, a market, or a library. Get ready to say three or four sentences about it. Use these sentence starters:
“In my community, there is a / an ______.”
“The location of it is ______.”
“People go there to ______.”
“I think this service is ______ (helpful / important / friendly).”
Record yourself, then listen back. Did you choose there is correctly, and did you speak in full sentences?
speaking.aiTutorPrompt: With an adult sitting beside me, listen to my four sentences about a local service and tell me whether I chose there is or there are correctly.

speaking.title: Speaking 2: Give Clear Instructions
speaking.instructionsAndModelLines:
Teach someone how to do a simple task — how to make tea, how to wash your hands, or how to send a message. Use imperatives and sequence words:
“First, ______.”
“Then, ______.”
“After that, ______.”
“Finally, ______.”
speaking.aiTutorPrompt: Ask an adult to stay with me, then check my spoken instructions and tell me whether every step begins with a sequence word and a comma.

speaking.title: Speaking 3: Twenty Questions: Guess the Job
speaking.instructionsAndModelLines:
Play this game with your AI tutor or your family while an adult is nearby. One person thinks of a community helper: a scientist, a teacher, a nurse, a postal worker or a shopkeeper.
The others ask yes/no questions to guess the job, such as “Do you deliver things?” or “Do you work with knowledge and books?”
The thinker may answer only “Yes, I do” or “No, I do not.”
Guess the job in twenty questions or fewer, then swap turns.
speaking.aiTutorPrompt: Play Guess the Job with me and my adult helper, answering only yes or no, then tell me which of my questions was the most useful one.

speaking.title: Speaking 4: Vocabulary Expert Interview
speaking.instructionsAndModelLines:
Choose six Unit 4 words and become the expert on each one.
Your partner asks a question about a word, and you answer in a complete sentence that uses it.
Try questions such as “What quantity of paper does the class need?” or “Whose priority is the newspaper?”
Swap roles after three words, and keep a tally of the words you both used accurately.
speaking.aiTutorPrompt: Sit with me and my adult helper and quiz me on six Unit 4 words, asking me to use each word in a full sentence before you give feedback.

speaking.title: Speaking 5: Explain and Respond
speaking.instructionsAndModelLines:
Explain one big idea from this unit, such as why a town needs a library service that travels.
Give your reason with because, then invite two follow-up questions from your listener.
Answer each question in one clear sentence, and add an example from “The Circular Plan” if it helps.
speaking.aiTutorPrompt: Listen while an adult is present as I explain one unit idea, then ask me two follow-up questions and tell me whether my reason with because was clear.

speaking.title: Speaking 6: Three-Minute Unit Talk
speaking.instructionsAndModelLines:
Plan and record a three-minute talk called “How my community shares news”.
Open with one sentence that names your topic, then give three connected ideas with an example for each.
Close by saying what you would change, and use First, Then and Finally so your listener can follow the order.
speaking.aiTutorPrompt: Time my three-minute talk while my adult helper listens, then tell me whether my opening, my three ideas and my closing were easy to follow.

writing.title: Writing 1: Instructions: “How to Share News in My Community”
writing.promptAndInstructions:
Write a set of instructions with at least four steps. Use a sequence word to begin each step, and use imperatives (action words). For example:
First, find real information. Then, write it clearly. After that, check your spelling. Finally, share it with your neighbours.
writing.modelText: First, ask three neighbours which news they need most. Then, write each fact in one short sentence. After that, check your spelling and erase every stray mark. Finally, pin the page where every family walks past.
writing.successCriteria: I wrote at least four steps; every step opens with a sequence word and a comma; every step uses an imperative verb; my steps run in a workable order.
writing.support: Say your four steps aloud first, and count them on your fingers before you write anything down.
writing.extension: Add a fifth step that tells the reader what to do when the news changes.

writing.title: Writing 2: Description: “A Circular Object in Nature”
writing.promptAndInstructions: Write four or five sentences describing something circular you have seen — the sun, the moon, a drum, a plate, a wheel. Begin with a descriptive starter: “This bright, circular moon is…”
writing.modelText: This bright, circular moon is a silver plate resting on the roof of the sky. Its plain white face carries no decoration at all, yet nobody in our town can stop looking at it.
writing.successCriteria: I began with a descriptive starter; I used circular and one further describing word; my singular noun matches a singular verb; I wrote four or five sentences.
writing.support: Draw your circular object first, then label three things you notice about its edge, colour and size.
writing.extension: Add a simile that compares your circular object with something else your reader knows.

writing.title: Writing 3: A Short Report: “My Town”
writing.promptAndInstructions: Write three or four sentences of true information about your town. You could write about its population, its location, or a service people use. Use the present simple for facts.
writing.modelText: Our town has a population of about nine thousand people. The market opens every morning beside the bus stop. A small clinic offers a free health service on Thursdays.
writing.successCriteria: I wrote three or four true facts; every verb sits in the present simple; my he, she and it verbs carry their s; I used one unit word about place or people.
writing.support: Collect your facts in a list before you write, and ask an adult to confirm that each one is true.
writing.extension: Add one sentence of opinion and label it clearly as an opinion rather than a fact.

writing.title: Writing 4: Connected Paragraph
writing.promptAndInstructions: Write a six-sentence paragraph about the way your community shares news. Begin with a topic sentence, and join your ideas with and, but or because.
writing.modelText: Our community shares news in three different ways. The market seller repeats whatever he hears, but the noticeboard keeps the message the same for everybody. I trust the noticeboard because its words never change on the way.
writing.successCriteria: My first sentence names the topic; I used and, but and because at least once each; every sentence adds new information; my paragraph runs to six sentences.
writing.support: Write your topic sentence first, then answer the questions how, when and why in turn.
writing.extension: Replace two ordinary verbs with stronger ones, and explain why the new verbs work better.

writing.title: Writing 5: Information Text
writing.promptAndInstructions: Write an information page called “Our Community Services” with a heading and five accurate facts. Use precise Unit 4 words, and check your spelling and punctuation before you finish.
writing.modelText: Our Community Services. The library lends fiction and true books to every child in town. The clinic gives health information on Tuesday mornings. The post office will deliver a letter to any village nearby.
writing.successCriteria: I gave my page a heading; I wrote five separate facts; I used at least three Unit 4 words; I proofread for spelling and full stops.
writing.support: Number your five facts in rough before you write them out neatly.
writing.extension: Lay the page out with a bulleted list, then say why that layout suits a reader in a hurry.

writing.title: Writing 6: Reflect and Improve
writing.promptAndInstructions: Choose one earlier piece from this unit. Revise three sentences, add two useful details, and explain in one sentence what you improved and why.
writing.modelText: I changed “The library is good” into “The library lends high-quality books to every village.” The new sentence carries real information, so my reader learns something from it.
writing.successCriteria: I chose an earlier piece; I revised three sentences; I added two useful details; I explained one improvement and gave my reason.
writing.support: Read your old work aloud and mark the sentence that tells your reader the least.
writing.extension: Ask a partner which change helped most, then write their reason beside your own.

service

Hunt for six details in this unit's texts, one for each question below.

assignments.title: Community and Communication learning portfolio
assignments.instructions:
Submit two pieces of work for the unit portfolio.
First, hand in Writing 1, your instructions for sharing news in your community. Then, record and upload Speaking 1, your description of a service in your community.
Marking guidance for the writing: use the Writing rubric, and award the top band only when every step opens with a sequence word followed by a comma and every step uses an imperative verb.
Marking guidance for the recording: use the Speaking rubric, and award the top band only when the learner uses there is and there are accurately, names the location of the service, and speaks in full sentences.
Return one improvement target for each piece and allow one resubmission.

quizzes.question: What does 'service' mean?
quizzes.options: A shape with a round edge all around. | The number of people in a place. | Help or work done for others. | To remove marks or mistakes.
quizzes.correctAnswer: Help or work done for others.
quizzes.explanation: A service is help or work done for others, like the free book service in Reading 1.

quizzes.question: What does 'knowledge' mean?
quizzes.options: Something more important than other things. | What you know or learn. | An amount or number of something. | To playfully annoy or make fun of someone.
quizzes.explanation: Knowledge is what you know or learn, which is why the library shelves are said to be packed with it.

quizzes.question: What does 'quantity' mean?
quizzes.options: An amount or number of something. | A place where something is. | To find or learn something new. | Stories that are made up and not real.
quizzes.correctAnswer: An amount or number of something.
quizzes.explanation: Quantity answers the question “how much?” or “how many?”, so it names an amount.

quizzes.question: What does 'erase' mean?
quizzes.options: To remove marks or mistakes. | To decide if something is good or bad. | Simple, not fancy or decorated. | Help or work done for others.
quizzes.explanation: To erase is to take marks away, which is what Maya does before she sticks her pages down.

quizzes.question: Choose the missing word from “The Circular Plan”: the librarian said kindly, “But good ______ always starts small.”
quizzes.explanation: The librarian is talking about the help the children want to give the town, so the word is service.

quizzes.question: Choose the missing word from “The Library That Came to Us”: Every Thursday, she loads books into a cart and travels to the villages to ______ them.
quizzes.explanation: Only an action word fits after to, and deliver means to bring something to a person or place.

quizzes.question: Choose the missing words from “The Town Meeting”: ______ a reading room with many books.
quizzes.options: There are | Is there | There is | Are there
quizzes.explanation: One reading room is a single thing, so the singular form there is opens the sentence.

quizzes.question: Choose the correct word: How ______ information did you find about our town?
quizzes.explanation: Information cannot be counted one by one, so it takes much rather than many.

quizzes.question: Choose the correct verb form: My brother ______ football at the weekend.
quizzes.explanation: My brother is a he, and the present simple adds s for he, she and it.

quizzes.question: Choose the missing connective: ______, share the finished page with your neighbours.
quizzes.explanation: Sharing the page is the last step, so the sequence connective Finally opens it.

liveSessions.title: Community and Communication: Launch, vocabulary and learning goals
liveSessions.beforeSession: Read the unit overview and learn the six words in Group 1.
liveSessions.agenda: 5 min welcome and Word Wall retrieval; 10 min teacher models the six Group 1 words; 15 min paired meaning match; 10 min learners set one personal unit goal; 5 min exit question.
liveSessions.afterSession: Tick the Group 1 words you can already use in a sentence.

liveSessions.title: Community and Communication: Reading fluency and comprehension
liveSessions.beforeSession: Read “The Library That Came to Us” once aloud and once silently.
liveSessions.agenda: 5 min choral reading of Reading 1; 10 min teacher think-aloud on the librarian's priority; 15 min paired comprehension with quoted evidence; 10 min compare Reading 1 with Reading 2; 5 min share one quotation.
liveSessions.afterSession: Answer the three questions on Reading 2 in full sentences.

liveSessions.title: Community and Communication: Grammar workshop and feedback
liveSessions.beforeSession: Attempt the practice in Grammar 1 and Grammar 2 before the session.
liveSessions.agenda: 5 min much and many warm-up; 10 min teacher models sorting countable and uncountable nouns; 15 min there is and there are drill in pairs; 10 min error hunt on modelled sentences; 5 min feedback on the two traps.
liveSessions.afterSession: Correct any grammar practice items you missed, and write out the rule you used.

liveSessions.title: Community and Communication: Dialogue, speaking and pronunciation
liveSessions.beforeSession: Prepare four sentences about a service near your home.
liveSessions.agenda: 5 min tongue-twister warm-up; 10 min model the service description with sentence starters; 15 min Guess the Job in threes; 10 min record instructions using sequence words; 5 min peer praise plus one target.
liveSessions.afterSession: Record Speaking 2 and listen back for the comma pause after each connective.

liveSessions.title: Community and Communication: Writing conference and revision
liveSessions.beforeSession: Bring your first draft of Writing 1 and Writing 3.
liveSessions.agenda: 5 min re-read the drafts; 10 min teacher models revising one weak step; 15 min writing conference in rotating pairs; 10 min silent editing for commas and imperatives; 5 min each learner records one improvement.
liveSessions.afterSession: Revise three sentences from your draft and note what you changed.

liveSessions.title: Community and Communication: Performance, assessment and reflection
liveSessions.beforeSession: Rehearse your three-minute talk once at home.
liveSessions.agenda: 5 min quiz warm-up; 10 min groups rehearse the three-minute talk; 15 min presentations to the class; 10 min unit quiz; 5 min self-assessment and preview of Unit 5.
liveSessions.afterSession: Complete the unit quiz and the self-assessment, then set one target for Unit 5.

teacherNotes.note: Model the new language aloud and check meaning before any independent work, then vary the response mode so learners can speak, draw or write their answers. Give specific feedback on complete sentences, quoted evidence and vocabulary precision. Keep an adult present whenever a learner opens the AI tutor or records audio; no child should work alone on the device, and recordings stay inside the class account.

Grammar answers. Practice 1: many, some, few, an, many. Practice 2: There is, There are, There is, There are, There is. Practice 3: bark, studies, swim, plays, revolves. Practice 4: The picture is painted by the artist; The game was won by the team; The homework was finished by the students; The books are delivered by the librarian every Thursday. Practice 5: First, Next, After that, Finally. Practice 6 Part A: Eat, Close, Do not talk, Help, Bring; Part B answers vary, so accept any describing word that matches a singular noun, such as “This friendly dog is playful.” Ask learners to read their AI-tutor feedback aloud to the adult beside them before they act on it, and remind them that the tutor checks work but never replaces the teacher session.

answerKey.answerOrGuidance: 1–c, 2–d, 3–e, 4–a, 5–b. If a learner swaps population and priority, ask which of the two you could count as people.
1. There is, 2. There are, 3. There is, 4. There are. Item 3 stays singular because information is uncountable.
1. many, 2. much, 3. many, 4. much. Books and people can be counted one by one; information and time cannot.
First, decide what you want to say. Then, write it down clearly. After that, check your spelling. Finally, give the message to the right person.

Things we share: service, information, knowledge, thought. Words that describe: circular, plain, quality, quantity. Things we do: deliver, discover, erase, tease. Accept a different sorting rule when the learner explains it in a full sentence.

1. Every Thursday. 2. A scientist. 3. Three: a reading room, a small clinic and an open hall. 4. Near the school gate, where every family walks past. 5. The word plain. 6. What people learn. Each answer needs the copied words plus one sentence of explanation.
Help or work done for others. Reading 1 shows it: the library runs a free book service for the whole town.
What you know or learn. The library shelves hold true books packed with knowledge for every reader.
An amount or number of something. Quantity answers how much or how many, while quality answers how good.
To remove marks or mistakes. Maya erases every mistake before she sticks her newspaper pages down.
service. The librarian tells Amal that good service always starts small, because helping others begins in small ways.
deliver. The librarian carries the books out to the villages, so the verb after to has to be deliver.
There is. A reading room is one single thing, so the singular form opens the sentence.
much. Information is uncountable, so it takes much, and it never adds an s either.
plays. My brother stands for he, and he, she and it always add the s in the present simple.
Finally. Sharing the page is the last step in the sequence, so it needs the closing connective and a comma.
